sections.name: File setup
sections.title: Accepted date patterns
sections.what: Lists the date patterns the app tries, in order, when a date is not already in standard form. They cover several day-month-year and month-day-year styles with and without times.
sections.why: Schedule exports come from different tools and regions, so several patterns are needed.
sections.watch_out: Patterns are tried in order, so a broad pattern placed early could match before a more specific one.

sections.name: normalize_date
sections.title: Converting a date to standard form
sections.what: Turns a date from any source into one standard text form with no time zone, or returns nothing when it cannot. Dates with a zone are converted to UTC first. Slash dates where day and month could be swapped are rejected.
sections.why: Likely reason: rejecting ambiguous slash dates avoids guessing the wrong month.
sections.watch_out: Dates such as 03/04/2020 are rejected, so a change to this rule changes which rows lose their dates.

sections.name: normalize_date_with_warning
sections.title: Converting a date and recording failures
sections.what: Does the same conversion, and when a non-empty value cannot be read, records a warning naming the field and row.
sections.why: So bad dates appear in the report instead of disappearing silently.
sections.watch_out: Long bad values are shortened in the warning text, so the full original value is not kept in the report.

sections.name: normalize_number
sections.title: Converting numbers
sections.what: Turns a text or number cell into a decimal, returning nothing for blank, unreadable or infinite values.
sections.why: Numeric fields such as lag hours arrive as text in many exports.
sections.watch_out: Unlike dates, a bad number returns nothing without any warning being recorded.

summary: Turns dates and numbers from schedule files into one standard form, and reports dates that cannot be read.
purpose: Makes dates from many export styles comparable and sortable, so the rest of the app can work with them.
why: Schedule exports use many date styles. A single standard form keeps the database consistent.
how: For a date, it first accepts real date objects, then standard ISO text, then a list of known patterns tried in order. Slash dates whose day and month could be swapped are rejected. A wrapper adds a warning when a non-empty value cannot be read. A separate function converts numbers and rejects blank or infinite values.
inputs: Raw cell values of any type, from spreadsheets, text files or XER records.
outputs: A date as standard text without a time zone, or nothing. Numbers as decimals, or nothing.
risks: Ambiguous slash dates are dropped rather than guessed, so some rows lose their dates. Times with a zone are converted to UTC, which shifts the stored time.
debug: If dates are missing, look for a matching invalid_date warning and check the raw value. For ambiguous dates, check whether the source uses day-first or month-first slashes.
